speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a matter of
privilege I should like to make a short explanation to the house with respect to an answer given to a question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I am reported as having answered his question in the following way as appears at page 959 of Hansard:
That question is, I suppose, merely for clarification, Mr. Speaker; but a hypothesis like that would not arise except in the case of war, real or apprehended. I can give the hon. member the assurance that for the duration of this parliament there is no thought at the present time that there need be any fear about war, real or apprehended.
When I received the transcript from the reporter, instead of the word "fear" there was the word "care"-"any care about war, real or apprehended". I do not reproach the reporter. It may be that in answering the questions which were being asked I was not speaking very distinctly. I corrected it to the word "fear", which I believe is the word I used. The advance copies had gone to the press galleries, however, and in quoting me in their newspapers the reporters quite properly used the text as it appeared in the advance copies. Apparently the newspaper reporters were not misled by it, because the headline given to the article in one newspaper was, "P.M. says no war for five years"; another newspaper said, "Five years' respite from fear of war foreseen by P.M". Nevertheless I thought it desirable that I state I did make a correction in the advance sheet for two reasons: one, to absolve the members of the press gallery from any implied reproach that might arise in the minds of people who compared their report with Hansard, and, second, to correct any impression that I might have said that preparation for war was not one of our cares at the present time. It is precisely because of the care being taken by the nations of the North Atlantic security pact that we are able to feel there is no fear or apprehension at this time. Principally I wanted it to be clear that the newspaper
reporters had justification for the use of the word "care" as it appeared in the quotation mentioned.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, October 20, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before adjourning the debate last night I had listened to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and I promised you, sir, that I would look it over in the meantime. I have done that, but I did not find many surprises in it. I was more shocked by the lack of additions to the speech than to read what I had read before. No budget has been practised so much and presented so often before being passed by the house. However, I feel that one cannot be unmindful of the great changes that took place during the past summer. The government's political success in the recent election is evidenced by its top-heavy majority in this house; in fact this is the first time that I have been almost completely surrounded by Liberals. Judging by their promising
The Budget-Mr. Rowe appearance I suppose one should call them statesmen. They are in front of you, behind you and on both sides of you. It is only natural that such a victory should bring to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his colleagues a sense of pride and satisfaction, indeed a sense of supreme confidence. With all due respect, one can say that at times we almost see a growing complacency coming out of that great victory. I sometimes wonder whether the victory was too great. I observe that the Minister of Finance seems happier than usual, and he is always happy. He seems to think that everything is all right. The Prime Minister himself is not even afraid of war for the next five years. Everything is rosy; everything is fine. I am reminded of a description that was once given of optimism-in saying this I mean no disrespect to hon. gentlemen whom I see in front of me and the sincerity of their purpose in serving this country. The man who gave the description said that the best explanation he ever heard of real optimism was a fellow who did not care what happened so long as it did not happen to him.
I say in all sincerity that I hope this allpowerful government, with an unprecedented number of members so ready to support it, will not develop an optimism so blind as not to observe the swiftly changing conditions on our economic front. If I should remind the Minister of Finance and his government of the possible far-reaching effects of conditions that have arisen lately to becloud our economic future with great uncertainties, I hope that such will not be recklessly regarded by those who sit to your right merely as what an opposition critic might be expected to do-to view with alarm for the sake only of alarm.
May I, however, assure the minister that no political motive actuates my remarks of today. The government have just won a general election. Indeed they have won it in no uncertain terms. Nothing I can say now can alter that situation. In fact it is apparent that anything I said before the election had no effect on it.
I am not unmindful of my responsibilities. I know that, despite what has been said or has not been said, or how much joy or applause there may be over the victory that some organizations have had, if our prosperity withers and dies because its roots have been torn out of the export markets on which it was based, then it will be the Canadian people as a whole who will suffer, without any distinction between Grit and Tory. None of us wants that to happen. Certainly I do not. And so today I speak not from any partisan motive; I speak with a keen sense

The Budget-Mr. Rowe of my responsibilities to the people of Canada. May I, however, ask the Minister of Finance, who needs no lecture from me on the great responsibility he carries, to concede to me the same sincerity in the lesser responsibility that is mine on this occasion. It is my hope to bring to the attention of this house the importance of the government's shedding at this time its political battledress and meeting in a business way the economic challenges of the hour.
The presentation of the annual budget has been an event of growing importance in the life and progress of our people. But, it is unique in the experience of this house to have, as I have said, a budget presented so often and practised so much before being passed by this House of Commons. In fact it has been back and forth in this house so often that it is almost worn out. It is also passing strange to me that while the economic face of literally the whole world has been changing swiftly during recent months, the government's fiscal proposals of today are only a rehash of the proposals that were unwrapped last March to dress the stage for the June election. It gave temporary cash relief. I am sorry that it did not go a little further in some respects and increase the exemptions of the poor man, as the party to which I have the honour to belong suggested. It gave cash relief to many Canadian taxpayers; therefore it had a distinct appeal to millions of taxpayers. It was, Mr. Speaker, a great election handbook, and served as a successful political expedient for a hasty election campaign. It lacked inspiration; it lacked the semblance of ability to observe obvious signposts that everyone else but the government saw last spring. It is obsolete now in the sense of meeting world conditions that have changed so much since. The minister and his advisers refused to see that the devaluation of the Canadian dollar would so soon be inevitable.
I do not propose to trace, in their elaborate and confusing detail, recent economic world events. Indeed, the rapid development of international bilateralism in trade, and diminishing overseas markets for our agricultural, forestry and fishery products, were obvious at that time-I speak of last March when this budget was first presented-to all hon. members of the house except the government itself.
The serious aspect of this misleading official attitude lies not alone in its strange lack of relationship to the facts, but especially in its striking similarity to the "wait and see" policy of the Liberal party just before and during the 1930 election. I can well recall that, despite the fact that a serious recession had started in the latter part of 1929, our

international trade channels were drying up, every elevator in Canada was filled with unsold wheat and every lumber yard was bursting with unsold lumber-despite these facts, at that time the Liberal party to your right, Mr. Speaker, were taking exactly the same attitude as they are taking today, even though it was followed by the serious economic depression of the early thirties.
During the recent election the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for whom I have a very high regard-I hope this is mutual, although I am not so sure-made certain statements. I do say of him that he is an optimist, and he is reasonably practical in everything else except his politics. But he should understand what is happening. I can remember being in certain parts of Canada while the minister was there-sometimes even in the same city. On every occasion he said that the outlook for Canada's trade was never brighter. I think he must have meant political trade, because his department of statistics only last week stated emphatically that for the first eight months of this year Canada's favourable balance of trade was less than it had been in any year since 1938. This was the condition, despite the fact that we had a greater volume of trade-and I will not overlook that, because the Minister of Trade and Commerce mentions it every time he is on his feet. He reminds me of the fellow who is doing more business-buying more and selling less. The statistics show that in the first eight months of 1949 we had an unfavourable trade balance-more unfavourable than we have had at any time since 1938. Despite the rosy pictures which were painted to the public, he must be honest.
Now. if I may refer to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)-I regret he is not in his seat today; and in passing let me say that I am glad he is restored to good political health-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not mean "political health"; I meant that I was glad he had been restored to good physical health. I know his political health is always pretty good. I think he will need good physical health in the future to endure the political associates he has had in the past.
Our farmers, from one end of Canada to the other, were told by the Minister of Agriculture that we had more markets for our agricultural products than we had agricultural products to sell. He was telling them this story to the point where they were eating twice as much as they did before-putting twice as much butter on their bread, and cutting their bacon twice as thick. The other evening in the house that same minister said

that during the first six months oi this year we sold to the United Kingdom, the greatest market we have had in the last fifty years, only one-sixth of the amount we sold the year before. And, despite all this brightness for the future, he added that now the United Kingdom did not care whether we sent them anything at all from our supply of foodstuffs. They would just as soon not have our bacon.
These trends which developed early this year were recklessly, or designedly, or both, disregarded by the government.
We all know that in recent weeks we have had a shocking currency devaluation on a broad international front. Some of us may be a little hazy as to the real reason for it, but none of us is doubtful as to what happened. We know how suddenly the United Kingdom devalued her currency-almost overnight, despite the fact that they had said they would not do it. They devalued their currency to the extent of thirty per cent. Then they followed with government-controlled currency-something like the hunter who chased the rabbit so far that it had to climb a tree, even though no other rabbit had ever done it.
We found the same thing here. Our great experts in the Department of Finance, the Minister of Finance himself as well, just laughed and said: "Me, too. Get on. We will go for the ride, whether it is a broncho ride or not. We shall have to take it". When the United Kingdom devalued its currency thirty per cent, all empire countries followed suit. The Argentine has devalued to the extent of forty per cent-with, it is true, extensive and highly complicated reservations. Canada has devalued to the extent of ten per cent, in other words twenty per cent less than the United Kingdom. It might have been made twenty, twenty-five or thirty per cent. They just got together and said: We have got to devalue; it might just as well be ten per cent as twenty per cent. Call it ten per cent, and let it go at that.
Canada devalued twenty per cent less than the United Kingdom, other commonwealth countries, and European countries associated in the sterling bloc. My hon. friends laugh, but they were not laughing over there in the east block-in fact they were all too much embarrassed to have good judgment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are all laughing at the Tory policy of devaluation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The inevitable results of these startling facts are bound to have a far-reaching effect on our economy. In the first place it will be obvious to any schoolboy economist that Danish bacon; Danish cheese; Scandinavian newsprint, pulp and paper; Australian and New Zealand dairy products:
The Budget-Mr. Rowe Argentine beef; electrical supplies from Sweden, and hundreds of other commodities from the sterling area nations will be available to the United Kingdom market at a price at least twenty per cent below their cost from Canada, the cost at which Canada could put her products there. That is obvious, surely, to everyone.
Despite our country's potential resources in her present period of post-war prosperity, we must not recklessly disregard these economic danger signs. We have had prosperity not because of but in spite of the present government. This is a great country. There is nothing mysterious about that. There is not one hon. member in front of me today who can give me a specific reason for our prosperity for which the government has been responsible. The government has been riding on the crest of world affairs, with the result that we have had prosperity. It has been kidding the people of Canada that it has given them that prosperity-just like the fellow who had his bank credit extended because he was out with the bank manager the night before, and was able to borrow more money than he had ever borrowed previously.
One-third of our whole national economy is dependent upon export trade. Every hon. member in the house knows that the United Kingdom is by far the greatest and the most important market we have for our agricultural surpluses. No other market exists on a scale sufficiently large to replace it. How long shall we continue to hold that market if our goods are priced twenty per cent above the prices of competing goods from sterling area sources?
The effect of this bureaucratic trading dollar creates in fact, if not in intention, for the first time in the history of empire trading relationships, an empire preference in the United Kingdom markets from which Canada alone of all empire countries is now excluded. That is automatically the effect of Britain and the commonwealth countries other than Canada devaluing to the extent of thirty per cent, while Canada devalues her dollar by only ten per cent. This gives them an advantage, as everyone can see, of twenty per cent right across the board. Non-British countries of the sterling area devaluing thirty per cent have for the first time a preference over Canada of twenty per cent in the British market-and Canada is the senior partner in the British commonwealth.
That is the position we are in today. It is a strange economic situation indeed, and I submit it will have many repercussions on business, unless the government makes some move other than that indicated in the dusty document presented last night.

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
The general prosperity we have recently been enjoying must not blind our vision, if we are to safeguard our economic future from these dangers. This is a twenty per cent disadvantage to the lumbermen of British Columbia, a twenty per cent disadvantage to the fishermen of the east, to the grain and meat producers of central Canada, to say nothing of the secondary industries-textile and farm implement industries. Can anyone say that that will not be a matter of serious concern to every person connected with the business life of this country? Since no one laughs at that, sir, I think at least hon. members to your right understand it.
Despite our present prosperity there are signs all around that we should not ignore. I say to the minister with all respect that, despite the changes in the budget, he has brought down off the shelf the very same program. There are a few exceptions. The sales tax is being taken off fuel oil-something which should have been done last year or the year before. In fact the government should have taken off all the sales tax. This budget seems to be just the same as it was last spring, something that blindly ignores our economic problems and consequently offers no solution so far as the long-range viewpoint is concerned. It is good, and I compliment the minister upon the splendid way he presented it. I also compliment his departmental officials upon the form of the document they have prepared. But after all, it is just something that an auditor might present. There is no more inspiration in it now than there was last spring. At that time it was full of political craftsmanship; today it is no less barren of economic statesmanship to meet changing conditions.
During the past decade, and directly as a result of the war, our agricultural markets have been largely dependent upon contractual bulk trading purchases. Much of our production went to supply the British market, often at prices far below world prices or far below what the British might have been able to pay. This policy was pictured to us as being one with great long-term advantages, but in fact it was the most reckless experiment in international trade in Canada's history. This policy of government-directed selling was admittedly at great cost to the Canadian farmer, but it was expected to give long-term stability so far as the United Kingdom market was concerned. Of course it also served to keep down the prices of the commodities the farmer had to sell.
Unfortunately a shortage of dollars and a return by Great Britain to her traditional markets in Europe, coupled with the adoption by that country of a policy of bilateral

trade agreements with soft currency countries, resulted in our loss of those markets to the point where the Minister of Agriculture is unable to assure the primary producers of this country of any contracts beyond the contract year 1950. The stark truth is that those markets which we hoped to hold after the war and which are essential to a healthy agricultural economy in this country, and have been for the past fifty years, are practically lost. Those markets are necessary to the economic health of this great basic industry. This costly bulk-trading experiment has proved a failure because it has choked off future market stability. Even during a time of rationed foodstuffs in Great Britain we have lost a market which we had held for fifty years.
The full effect of this has not been felt, because there are still a few contracts. We have the benefit of support from the European recovery plan and the Marshall fund in the purchase of our wheat, but these markets have a definite limitation because the Marshall plan is scheduled to finish in 1952. The discontinuance of purchases in Canada through this medium will have a serious effect upon this country unless an alternative means of retaining these or other markets is rapidly found.
The alternative market which we have been able to secure for our surplus production in the United States is not at all assured for the future. Surpluses are now beginning to appear in that country, which means that our ability to sell there will become less favourable as time goes on. Our similarity of production, coupled with the capacity of the United States to produce, makes that market most hazardous at best.
The history of trade shows that our most secure agricultural markets for the last fifty years have been found in Europe, and especially in the United Kingdom. These traditional markets for Canadian products have been diverted to eastern Europe and other commonwealth countries under long-term bilateral agreements. The problem of trade in this sphere is made more difficult by the fact that these long-term bilateral trade agreements, such as Britain's five-year agreement with Poland, project far past the time in the future when it was hoped that trade channels would have been cleared of the obstructions resulting from dislocations caused by the war. As a nation with its agricultural economy dependent upon the export of surplus production to reasonably stable markets, we can no longer ignore the fact that the trend today is in a direction adverse to the future welfare of this country's basic industry.
Last week the representatives of ten western European countries met at Rome to

prepare a report to be submitted to the world conference of the food and agricultural organization scheduled to meet in Washington next month. The substance of the report which will be presented at that time is that the western European countries purchase more of the food they must import from eastern Europe and less from this continent. In other words the system of bilateral trade, which now expresses itself through some three hundred bilateral trade agreements among European nations, and which is slowly but surely closing its door to exports from this country, is to continue and constitute the order of trade for some indefinite period in the future. This should cause serious thought on the part of all businessmen and farmers in Canada.
Countries within or under the shade of the iron curtain are replacing Canada in the British market, in many cases under bilateral deals which extend up until 1955. Bacon which was formerly supplied by Canada is now being obtained from Denmark, Poland, Hungary, and other countries. Our present cheese contract for 50 million pounds is for an amount lower than our sales in this market at any time during the past fifty years. Our contract for eggs calls for the purchase of only three-fifths of our exports to the British market last year, which were below what they had been the year before-and this at a time when the farmers of other European countries are increasing their sales in the British market.
This market, which took as high as a million cases a year of evaporated milk and 8 million pounds annually of milk powder, has been lost to Poland, Australia, New Zealand, Denmark, and other countries. It is not surprising that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford)-who by the way, has never been accused of not giving the Minister of Finance and his party full support-stated in the house the other night that this phase of agriculture has become the orphan of the dairy industry. That is even worse than anything that has been said on this side of the house. The hon. member stated that there were 2,500 farmers in his county who depended upon this branch of agriculture for their living. He said that 8 million pounds of evaporated milk have been stored in the county because there is absolutely no market at home or abroad. I wonder at the hon. member bringing this matter to the floor of the house and not taking it up with the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who say they have markets for more than we can produce. I think it would have been better to take it up there. If those ministers had such markets during the election, I would suggest that in
The Budget-Mr. Rowe fairness to the 2,500 farmers in Leeds, some of whom may have supported the present hon. member for that riding, the hon. member should ask the permission of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture to use their names to set up a Howe-Gardiner sales corporation in Brock-ville to sell the 8 million pounds of milk now in storage. Those ministers are the past-master salesmen who during the election said that they could sell more than we could produce. It is not long since the election. I wonder if something along that line might not provide a lead for the business mind of the hon. member for Leeds.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Speak a little louder; the minister does not hear you.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to disturb him. I think it is just as well that I do not. He is exercising a parliamentary privilege. I will not enlarge on that, but I have listened to him often when I would rather have been doing something else.
A similar situation exists with respect to the markets we previously held for beans, poultry, canned salmon, flax fibre, fruits and fruit juices, vegetables, oats, barley, and numerous other agricultural products. Probably when the Minister of Trade and Commerce gets into action he may find markets for those products, but nobody else seems to know where they are going to be sold under present conditions.
In the field of non-metalliferous mining and quarry products, our exports to the United Kingdom markets have dropped to one-third of their 1938 volume. In the field of tobacco exports, Canada built up a considerable market in the United Kingdom, as everyone knows. Last year our exports of tobacco to that market were reduced to approximately 12J million pounds from the 22J million pounds we sold them the year before. At the same time Turkey, which had exported less than half a million pounds in 1947, increased that to over 10 million pounds in 1948, taking the market that we formerly had for our tobacco growers.
A similar story prevails with regard to leather and leather products. Our exports to the British market fell from over 5,000 hundredweight in 1947 to less than 1,000 hundredweight in 1948.
As I have already stated, the full impact of this loss of markets has been temporarily deferred by our finding markets in the United States of America. There is now every indication of a surplus of many articles in the United States, and the likelihood of holding those markets is very doubtful, as it always has been. To find new markets for surplus Canadian production, or have the domestic

The Budget-Mr. Rowe market absorb even a considerable portion without disrupting trade, presents a considerable problem indeed.
Efforts are made from time to time by members of the government to detract from the disastrous implications in our present trend of foreign trade by placing the entire responsibility on the shortage of dollars experienced by British purchasers. But that answer does not offer any solution. Since the close of the war, agricultural machinery has been a large export factor, but now the greater devaluation of sterling compared with that of the dollar is making the export of Canadian farm machinery very doubtful. As a result, as the minister knows, unemployment is beginning to mushroom in these important machinery factories.
The government's policy of holding the Canadian dollar at an artificial valuation is now anchoring the strategically important ocean shipping industry. Even before the United Kingdom and Scandinavian countries devalued their currencies, Canadian oceangoing bottoms were operating on a slender margin, as the minister knows, compared with shipping under other flags. Owing to higher wages, higher shipbuilding costs, higher standards of crew treatment, and higher operating efficiency, we believe, Canada faces a most difficult situation. To this difficult picture competing rates are reduced by thirty per cent, whereas Canadian rates can drop only by 10 per cent to maintain the same equilibrium. Thus, today, in every seaport of the nation, ships of Canadian registry are becoming known as "the mothball fleet". They are dropping their anchors and paying off their crews. They are unable to compete for cargoes against vessels of Scandinavian, British and other registry. The government certainly will not deny that several of its leading ministers have from time to time, as other hon. members have, emphasized the importance of our great merchant marine in the carrying of ocean cargo. Indeed, during the last war the part that the merchant marine played was the pride of many Canadians; in fact, many have said that victory would not have been possible had it not been for the great services it rendered. Today, because of the currency policy of the country, we find shipping services being crippled, which emphasizes the imperative necessity of getting down to solid common sense so far as currency values are concerned.
What has been the effect of this violent currency change upon our industries which cater to the domestic market? Clearly one effect of the British devaluation of thirty per cent is the equivalent of a cut in the tariff against the British goods. Can our textiles, our rubber and leather goods industries, our

footwear industry, and a whole host of others, compete with British tariffs thus cut down to almost nothing overnight? In addition they pay lower wages than we do.
For the past few moments I have been tracing-and I know that some will think haphazardly-the effects of devaluation on the major aspects of our national economy and the business life of the country. No one realizes more than I do that I have fallen far short of exhausting this subject, which today is bothering everyone who thinks seriously about our national economy. I have dealt with only a few concrete examples, because time prevents me from dealing with many others.
May I now discuss briefly what I consider to be the vital question underlying the whole situation, namely, what is the road that has led us into our present difficulties? Why have we had to resort to devaluation so suddenly and to this reckless tampering with our currency? It will be clear to all of us that we arrived at our recent crossroad of devaluation wholly and solely because some years ago, accepting the advice of experts, the government adopted what is known as foreign exchange control. If we had not retained foreign exchange controls after the war there would have been no problem of devaluation harshly and ruthlessly confronting Canadian industry almost overnight. Our dollar would have been fluctuating in accordance with the balance of our import and export trade, and would have been regulating that balance automatically from day to day. Its value would not be an arbitrary one fixed by some government decree. We have said that repeatedly, and now that the election is over, surely the government believe it. Their actions would indicate they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then the actions are misleading because the government believe very strongly in foreign exchange control.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yours mostly have been. Its value would not be so arbitrarily fixed. I wonder if members of the house have paused long enough to realize just what it is that we do when we withdraw our dollar from the free currency market and place it under foreign exchange controls, or government decree. In effect we simply delegate to a departmental official, who neither buys, sells nor manufactures, the task of placing a rigid arbitrary value on our currency, independently of what it will buy or sell from day to day in the market places of the world. Actually that is all that we do. But it should be obvious to us that no government official or group of men should be asked- even with the Minister of Finance being called in-to be expert enough to price the

dollar exactly, or even approximately at its real value, over any long period of time. If by some freak one of them had such genius- and I refer to departmental officials for whom I have all respect-he would do much better elsewhere; if, by some even more mysterious freak, there might be one of those master minds among those you see to your left and right, Mr. Speaker, one who could fix the value of the dollar exactly where it should be, the Prime Minister could not keep him in his government. He would be too successful somewhere else. Anyone who had that type of supreme genius would be able to make a far greater fortune for himself by pricing the stock market than being a mere dollar pricer for the government. But no such expert exists either in the departments or in those surrounding the minister. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) looks very bright, but I do not think even he would undertake that sort of thing. Mr. Speaker, I sometimes wonder why, in view of that fact, we continue to entrust the valuation of our currency to government and political decree. Such action is bound to bring us in a period of time to the necessity of rude and disturbing adjustment, the shock of which may indeed mean fortunes for a few and insolvency for those unprepared for the violent storm that follows.
That is the ultimate fate of all currency controls. None of them has ever led to expansion of trade. That is their record. To expect success for the first time from such a policy in Canada is dangerous and reckless optimism. I realize, of course, that such a view is heresy in the eyes of the so-called experts. Ever since these experts first succeeded in binding us in the chains of currency controls, they have sought to wrap the entire subject of foreign exchange in mystery and to establish it as far too technical a subject for comprehension by the ordinary lay mind. To a large extent their efforts along this line have been only too successful in increasing their popularity amongst those who do not understand the problem.
All my life, regardless of any other interests, I have been a practical farmer. I have been schooled in the belief that the Canadian farmer is equipped with the intelligence to understand any problem upon which his own economic welfare may ultimately depend. Consequently, I refuse to accept the subject of foreign exchange policy as a mystery too intricate for lay Canadians to concern themselves with. I simply translate it into the homely terms of my farming background. I realize that when the government guesses at the price our dollar should bring in the markets of the world, it is only a guess. To me it is like the farmer who takes
The Budget-Mr. Rowe his eggs to market and insists on pricing them at ninety cents per dozen, regardless of the fact that all the other farmers in the market stalls around him are selling eggs at seventy-five cents per dozen. Naturally, the public is not going to buy from him until he is willing to accept the prevailing market price. Similarly, foreign countries will not buy from us if they can get the same goods cheaper elsewhere. They will not pay the extra twenty per cent to secure our currency, except in respect to goods that they can get nowhere else. The range of such goods is far too narrow, Mr. Speaker, to be made the basis of a prosperous foreign trade. It is infinitesimal in comparison with the broader range of our national economy and trade.
May I express the same truth in another way? My common sense convinces me that we cannot obtain more for our dollar than it is worth. The way to find out what it is actually worth is not to have the government write and tie its price tag upon it, but to take it into the market-place to discover what world traders will give in return for it. Only when we release our dollar from exchange controls and allow it to function freely will we have assurance, not only as to its real worth, but also as to the basic soundness of our own economy. For a sound currency the meeting of the daily market test of free exchange against other currencies acts as a balance wheel or regulator of a nation's economy. It must not be too dear to prevent other nations buying from Canada. It must not become too cheap to prevent Canada using it to buy needed supplies abroad. The narrow fluctuations of each day warns that it is departing from equilibrium. Imports or exports then adjust themselves to bring it back into balance. That is how simply the free dollar works. It has worked that way throughout history whenever it has been given a chance unaffected by government decree and monopoly.
By contrast, Mr. Speaker, exchange control has never worked. In essence, it is a tampering with a nation's currency. When kings used to tamper with the currency in the old days, they lost their heads. Today whenever governments try tampering with their people's currency under the pretext of controlling exchange, the people invariably end up with an economic headache. Today we are discovering that from sad experience.
The question now arises as to whether or not during the past decade, under the system of state-controlled bulk purchasing which existed, we have lost much of our ability to buy and sell in competitive export markets. It is questionable whether or not we have forgotten how to do business by trading. Our loss of traditional markets for Canadian

The Budget-Mr. Rowe exports, and our failure to facilitate purchases of United Kingdom exports in short supply in Canada and which we have had to buy with scarce American dollars, warrants the immediate attention of the government. True, we have set up what is called a continuing trade committee and a dollar-sterling trade board. I think this indicates that the people outside are becoming so alarmed that they are going to do something on their own. I believe the government has given its blessing to that effort. I do not know how the government could have done otherwise because it has not done much about the problem. These efforts are creditable but are, at best, only exploratory efforts.
Our loss of traditional markets is of such concern to our future economic welfare in Canada that I suggest the problem be dealt with at top government levels at the earliest opportunity. Towards this end, I suggest that the Canadian government inaugurate steps for the holding of an empire trade conference at the earliest possible date. I make this suggestion, not with any idea of reverting to a policy of tariffs or violating our commitments under the Geneva trade agreements or the Annecy agreements, but in the firm conviction that this problem if tackled by top government representatives from all parts of the commonwealth can result in material advantage to all countries concerned.
The great British commonwealth of nations, Mr. Speaker, is not written off yet as one of the greatest trading forces in the world and is one in which Canada should be interested. Over five hundred million people are involved, and Britain has stood the longest of any of the world's great international organizations. In the early 1930's, an empire conference was held in Ottawa, following that debacle of the depression. I believe the result of it has been overlooked too often, Mr. Speaker, even by some of those to your right whose judgment, at times, is sound. Those people should know that no effort has been made in trade relations that has been so discounted as the British empire trade agreements of 1932 which were made in Ottawa. If anyone doubts me, Mr. Speaker, then I would ask him to look at the record. It would be found that inter-trade within the commonwealth in the five years following these empire trade agreements increased no less than fifty-two per cent.
We are a part, Mr. Speaker, of this great international institution, and despite our close association with the great republic to the south, we must not neglect a market that has been our best outlet for fifty years. The inroads being made today by communists or communist-dominated countries into

traditional Canadian markets prove conclusively, I submit, the possibilities and advisability of such a conference as I have suggested. These clear challenges to our long-range economic security and national defence far transcend the shifting fortunes of government or opposition parties. They demand more than a nonchalant political approach. They demand our best business approach. The prosperity we enjoy now must be weighed in the light of stern realities of world conditions. Our optimism as to its continuity must be tempered by the powerful factors that can alter it so abruptly. If we are to build a firm economic foundation for the future, we must discount the artificial financial stimulants so simple to apply in good times but so difficult to practise in hard times. We must plan for that day when we will be on our own economically, when the United States Marshall plan may no longer supply United States dollars for our overseas customers to pay for our wheat and bacon.
I have no doubts about the potential greatness of Canada. I am not preaching blue ruin, but I have had enough experience in farming to know that, no matter how prosperous you may be now, it is well to look ahead. There is an old saying about the goose hanging high. But no matter how high the goose may hang, a man would be more than I should like to describe parliamentarily if he did not look into the future to see how this prosperity, artificial or otherwise, can be sustained and to what degree. I am not preaching that we have not prosperity. I have emphasized the fact that we have.
I have no doubt about the potential greatness of Canada, with her resources and her possibilities. Under sound common-sense development the energy, genius and initiative of her people are sufficient to provide an ever-advancing standard of living for more people and greater national security for peace and prosperity in the future. No other country today has such latent strength with so few people. The government of today has the greatest opportunity of any government since confederation, despite the problems I have pointed out. Temporary expedients for political power are now no longer necessary to a government that enjoys an embarrassing numerical power surplus, even if some of that support has been gained by astutely discounting free enterprise itself. Of course it would be doubtful sportsmanship on my part to suggest to the government that they should repent at this time after such a great victory; but with all respect I suggest that with the serious economic and defence problems that stare us in the face and scream for solution, the hour has struck when every hon. member

of this house, no matter to what party he belongs, should shed his political armour, put on his working clothes, and face the difficult trade realities that so stubbornly ridicule our folly.
The members of any other sound executive board would stop and take stock at this time, and count the costs. If we are to safeguard our growth and development in this country we must start playing more economics and a little less politics.
In the field of social legislation we have progressed far in the years that are past, especially since 1920. We have not reached the peak of our endeavour or even the desire of our people in this regard. All parties in this house subscribe to the objective of making benefits under welfare legislation as adequate as possible. However, Mr. Speaker, this nation must have keen regard for the costs of those services, and our abilities to meet them as permanent fixed charges against the changing fortunes of our economy.
Social security expenditures in the present year will exceed $800 million. That amount is double the total tax and non-tax revenue of Canada in the year 1935. In periods of prosperity, with the high national income we now have, the costs of these services may not be too burdensome. There is no one in Canada so unkind as to suggest that we should not do all we can in the way of these services as long as we can pay for them. But we must realize the costs of these services and make sure that they are not too great a burden on our economy.
We have no assurance that the national income will continue at its present high peak. We have, however, a fair indication of the social services that the people of this country demand and that the people who are in politics want to give. I think the time has come for a careful re-examination of our whole approach to the question of financing the social security measures we now have and which, as a nation, we must sustain and expand in the future.
To the extent that unemployment insurance, old age pensions and family allowances may tend to keep up purchasing power, they will help this nation to meet problems that arise in a depressed economy. But let there be no illusion in the minds of our people about how social security measures are financed. They are paid for out of national income which, in reality, is the product of those who work. In other words, these services are, in the final analysis, made possible and are maintained, not by the government but by the national production and initiative of the Canadian people. Let us recognize that if it were not for the great wealth of our natural resources, combined with the
The Budget-Mr. Rowe industry and initiative of our great people, we as a nation, with such a small population, could never begin to take care of social security obligations involving $800 million this year. This is saying nothing of the welfare state that is suggested and the social services that many of us believe should be brought into being. There can be no true or continuing security for anybody without production of wealth, production that gives work, and opportunity for work that gives production.
The Minister of Finance closed his remarks last night by citing the tax reductions made each year since 1945. These reductions were, in the minds of the Canadian people, both welcome and necessary, and many of them were overdue. What the minister did not point out, however, was the relationship of government expenditures, or cost of government, to the gross national income of the country. If he was in his private business office, these are matters with which, I submit, he would deal, in any business concern he might be connected with. I do not mean to say that he is not just as honest in his public service, but he has so many miscellaneous problems that it makes it difficult for him to practise exactly the same in politics as you often have to practise in business. Now that the election is over I hope that the minister will get back to sound business practices.
I find that in 1938 our expenditures totalled $553 million. That was a great deal of money. At that time our national income was $5,100 million. This year our expenditures, according to what the Minister of Finance said last night, are going to be around $2,400 million. The national income that is flourishing so greatly, that he and the Minister of Trade and Commerce said during the election campaign was mushrooming all across the country-they were getting volume and dollars so mixed up that the people believed they were producing more volume than they ever did before-is approximately $13 billion. That is a great deal of money.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sixteen billion.

I know that two or three billion do not make much difference to hon. gentlemen opposite. Perhaps it has grown in the last few days. I am not like the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who one night said that a million dollars did not seem to matter. I do not want to imply that I am so reckless that a billion or two does not seem to matter much. But I do know this, Mr. Speaker. Our national income this year is up two and one-half times what it used to be in days gone by, but our national expenditure for the same period is up four and one-third

The Budget-Mr. Rowe times. It is only a matter of mathematics for some of the experts in the Department of Finance to figure out how long we can go on in that way, where no matter how much you get in you are paying more out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If we have to fight many more wars, we shall be worse off.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) says there is not going to be any more war for five years, so my friends have nothing to worry about in that regard.
Buoyant revenues, resulting in surpluses for the past few years, have resulted in a decreased attention to the need of strict economy in administering government services. Our commitments for social welfare measures now on the statute books and as well measures contemplated and projected, plus the interest charges on our public debt, are inescapable.
To meet the danger of such a situation loading the economy of this country with a burden it is not yet prepared to bear, I would make the following recommendations in the sincere hope that this government, no matter how complacent they may feel with the great majority behind them, will give them every possible consideration. I would like to suggest to the Minister of Finance:	One, the
inauguration at once of a government-wide economy policy without creating undue hardship or hindering the economic development of this country. As a suggestion, I would like to see a survey undertaken to ascertain the percentage cost of the collection of revenue today as compared with the last year before the war. Two, in order to assure the ability of this nation to sustain the social security policies, the various price support programs, and the other fixed charges of government to which we are committed, and as well provide the necessary defence preparedness program Canada must have-no matter who says we are not going to have any trouble, I believe it is most essential-I suggest the inauguration, in co-operation with the provinces, of a national development program.
While economies can and should be undertaken at once, I do not believe that the effect of these economies alone, no matter how rigid they may be, would be sufficient to meet the staggering burden of increasing fixed charges on our national economy. We must increase production and if we are to stabilize our economy and make a sound recovery this must be accomplished. This can only be achieved by the genius, enterprise, and thrift of our people in expanding and developing more rapidly the great natural resources of our country. That is the only way we can develop our resources as rapidly as we should.

If we are to maintain our high standard of living, an adequate policy of social welfare, a high percentage of employment which is desirable to us all, and adequate defence preparedness, which no one wants neglected even if it means more taxes, then we must direct our efforts to those avenues that will create new wealth. To do these things we need a policy of development as much as we needed it in the days before 1900. Only a new accelerated production will create this national income sufficient to sustain those things to which the government now stands committed. We have built great structural buildings for a small population of about 13,000,000. If we are to live better than anyone else, be happier and nicer to each other and do all the things we want to do, we have to enlarge and expand our genius, initiative and hard work to develop the greatest resources that any similar number of people have ever enjoyed. Fortunately, in this country we are endowed with great resources. The oil and coal fields of Alberta, the mining fields of Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland, the productivity and diversification of the agricultural industry of our provinces, the large timber areas of British Columbia and other parts of Canada, coupled with the industrial expansion of this nation, have in the last decade divulged more wealth than this country ever dreamed of.
The challenge now is one of fuller utilization of these resources, and the leadership for this must be encouraged rather than discouraged by the government. That leadership, however, must not be restrained by government controls and currency restrictions. It must not be restrained by the stagnant hand of socialism. Commitments must not be increased further in the future without serious regard for the fixed charges that are involved so that we may be able to meet them in times of recession as well as in times of prosperity.
I suggest that when the Prime Minister reorganizes his cabinet, which I understand he is going to do immediately following this session, he give consideration-
