I hear a voice from British Columbia. Perhaps the hon. member is ready to take it on, I do not know. I hope they will direct their full attention to the development of the great resources of this country.
Canada needs foreign capital. As the minister knows so well, she needs enterprise and development. Our fiscal and taxation policies must be sound and attractive to those within and without Canada whose faith in our great potential resources prompts them to venture and risk their savings in the enterprise of our country's expansion.
In order to assist the government to try and open up greater opportunities in this country, to try to broaden the basis of taxation and to try to have our great resources flourish and expand so that the people can get the most out of them and this country reach her destiny, in order to assist the government in that and in safeguarding our economic security and progress generally, I beg leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris):
That all the words of the resolution after the first word "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets that the government has failed to take effective measures to prevent the present decline in our trade with the sterling area and is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of inviting the nations of the commonwealth to a conference in the immediate future for the purpose of working out arrangements to preserve and enlarge those traditional markets on which jobs and opportunities for Canadians very largely depend.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before I begin my remarks this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I should like to take exception to a report which appears in today's Toronto Star and which was just handed to me. It reads as follows:
To serve their own political ends Progressive Conservatives and the C.C.F. are conniving to "block, hinder or delay" the Liberal government's low-rental housing program, Perry Ryan said last night at his Toronto-Greenwood campaign headquarters. The Liberal contestant in Monday's by-election said both parties "automatically" opposed the government's plan for rental relief because it had been offered by the Liberals. They were against the program, he said, "because they would rather see appalling housing conditions continue than admit the Liberal government had a good plan to correct conditions."
I say, Mr. Speaker, that such a statement is a deliberate misrepresentation. Whether the Liberal candidate is a lawyer or not he should look at the libel laws of Canada,
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher because we may have occasion to use them if he does not watch his statements. In the C.C.F. group in this house there are thirteen members. I believe the Liberal party has 186. The candidate in Greenwood gives our thirteen members a great deal of credit if he suggests that we can hold up the Liberal party's housing program. This group has asked for low-rental subsidized housing ever since the end of the war. If the city of Toronto has not low-rental subsidized housing today it is the fault, not of our thirteen members, but of the Liberal party, the party of which he is a candidate. I am sure that responsible Liberal leaders would not approve of the statement he made last night in Toronto, and on behalf of this group I wish to take the strongest possible exception to it.
At the outset of my remarks this afternoon I must admit frankly that this is not the easiest budget in the world to criticize, for two reasons: It is difficult, first, because it was originally presented to the house more than six months ago, and secondly because, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) pointed out last night, the government which presented it has since that date received an overwhelming mandate from the people of Canada.
May I say however that I am privileged to be speaking this afternoon-even though possibly my hon. friend from Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) will wonder why I am doing so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I certainly do.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the purpose of the budget was to win an election for the Liberal party, or to help win it, then very obviously it has been a successful budget.
A few weeks before the election was announced the minister and his colleagues were able to give a great many gifts to a great many people. For instance, the minister was able to promise tax relief to hundreds of thousands of Canadians. He was able to increase old age pensions for a large number of old age pensioners. Indeed I believe he was able to promise the building of a new bridge in the Cape Breton area. Thousands of prairie farmers were refunded millions of their own money in the form of participation certificates.
And so it went. The minister and his colleagues were able to give many things to many people; and from the viewpoint of the Liberal party the budget can be described only as a clever, effective and well-timed election-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Bribe.

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-bribe. That is as good a word as any-or an election instrument. Certainly the minister was most successful, in a political sense.
However the election is now over and I think that today we might leave the political aspects of the document behind. Some people look upon the budget only as a balance sheet of the nation's affairs. If it shows a surplus, then for the most part those people consider it a fairly good one. I know most hon. members would consider such a viewpoint to be superficial. It seems to me that, first and foremost, an effective budget should contain proposals to meet the major economic problems facing the nation. In our opinion this budget before us today fails to do that.
Probably the most critical problem facing Canada at this time is our steadily developing trade crisis. Most authorities agree, I believe, that before many months go by, the standard of living of most Canadians might well be affected by that trade crisis. As reported at page 1802 of Hansard for March 22, 1949, when the minister presented the budget, he said:
The Canadian government has taken and will continue to take all feasible steps to encourage the expansion of British trade with Canada.
I feel I must challenge the validity of that statement. The C.C.F. group in parliament feels that, far from taking all feasible steps to meet the deteriorating trade picture, the government has been apathetic, indeed it has been negligent, in its efforts to improve British-Canadian trade. In our opinion that negligence and apathy is the chief shortcoming of the budget we are discussing today.
It is so evident that Canada is facing a trade crisis that I do not think I have to labour the point this afternoon. During the recent election, as the hon. member who preceded me said, many cabinet ministers in various parts of the country made election speeches stating that Canada, after all, really had no trade problems.
For instance, the Regina Leader-Post carries the following report of a radio speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture:
He asserted that, despite claims to the contrary, neither the home nor export markets were in danger of being lost.
Then a press report of the minister's speech delivered at Simpson, Saskatchewan, a few days later states:
Market is Safe Gardiner Says
Hitting out at political opponents who have been accusing the Liberal government of losing Canada's markets. Agriculture Minister J. G. Gardiner declared at a public meeting here Wednesday night there is no truth in such suggestions because Canada has no surplus of farm products to sell.

I ask hon. members to note the headline, "Market is Safe Gardiner Says." That was a few weeks before the election. Then the election came along. I happened to pick up an issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail a few weeks later, and I find that in this article the minister is reported to have been again talking about markets. This time however he had a different story. The article is headed "Gardiner Unsure Canada Can Hold U.K. Food Markets", and states:
We are trying to maintain Canada's markets in Britain, but there is no certainty that we can do so.
Please note those two statements: Gardiner before the election, "market is safe"; Gardiner after the election, "market is unsure". What happened in that time to change the situation?-unless it was the election. If I did not know the Minister of Agriculture so well, if I did not know his reputation, I would almost think he was trying to delude the electors of Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He would not do that!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Some of the other ministers were equally confident of trade prospects during the election. On June 18 at New Westminster we heard from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). A Canadian Press dispatch carries the headline -"Howe Tells B.C. Liberals He's Stuck for Something to Sell". Then, over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation stations, on June 3, the minister said, as reported in the Toronto Daily Star:
Anyone who suggests trade relations between Britain and Canada are deteriorating is talking nonsense.
Certainly the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his speeches before the election simply oozed confidence. I wonder if his statements were in accordance with the facts. I wonder if things were as good as he pictured them. Certainly many people in Canada did not think they were.
Here is what the Canadian exporters association had to say-around the time the minister was speaking-and I quote from the Montreal Gazette:
The federal government is charged by the . . . Canadian exporters' association with misleading the public as to Canada's export position through false statistics and unqualified announcements of trade progress.
The government is further charged with allowing continued and accelerating deterioration of the country's position and is asked to take constructive steps to recover a loss in world markets.
As a result . . . Canadian producers and the people of Canada are largely unaware of the markets Canada has lost abroad, of the danger that threatens our export trade.
That is not the statement of a C.C.F. member, or a C.C.F. organization; rather it

is the statement of a group of businessmen whose duty it is to look after the Canadian exports.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce went back last night to address the same body. I believe he spoke at a banquet, but this time he had an entirely different story to tell. In effect he told them that the situation was pretty serious. I do not think the minister would suggest that, as he put it, the Canadian exporters association was talking nonsense when it said that the trade crisis was deteriorating. When the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce told the people of Canada several months ago that our traditional markets are safe, I do not think they were speaking correctly. They know now, as they knew then, that our traditional markets-particularly our market in Great Britain-have never been in greater jeopardy.
Our markets in Britain have been shrinking ever since the close of the war. This has been true particularly of our manufactured and processed goods, upon which we depend so fully to maintain full employment. But it has also been true of such pre-war staples as farm products, lumber products and the products of our fisheries. Our exports to Britain have been shrinking despite the fact that we have been making substantial gifts and loans to Britain. They have been shrinking despite the fact that the Americans have granted heavy ERP aid to the British to finance purchases in Canada.
As a matter of fact Britain today is buying from countries in western Europe many of the products which formerly she obtained in Canada. The causes of our present trade difficulties are well known to most hon. members, and I shall not take the time of the house to go into them. Prior to the war Britain bought three times as much from Canada as we purchased from her, but because of the devastation of war she is no longer in a financial position to do that. Great Britain has been forced by harsh realities to buy from those countries that will buy from her. It is not a case of ingratitude, as was suggested by some hon. members early this session; the fact is that she has not been able to trade with us on the old basis simply because she lacks Canadian dollars to do so. Unless we can do something to let Great Britain earn more Canadian dollars, then the chances are that our primary markets will disappear to an even greater extent.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and other ministers have been telling the country that all is well, that our trade markets are safe. How can they
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher reconcile those statements with some of the statements British officials have made when visiting this country? On his trip a few months ago Harold Wilson, the president of the British board of trade, is reported in a Canadian Press dispatch of May 13 as having said:
We are faced with the knowledge that Marshall dollars will progressively decline between now and 1952.
So unless we manage to push up our earnings of United States and Canadian dollars faster than offshore dollars decline, we shall be able to buy less from Canada in future rather than more . . . even maintenance of the present rate will be dependent on a great expansion of our exports to Canada.
The Right Hon. Ernest Bevin told us precisely the same thing when he was here in Ottawa several weeks ago. Prime Minister Attlee, Sir Stafford Cripps and other British statesmen have told us, not once but many times, that the only way we can avoid this trade deterioration is by buying more British goods.
Last evening the minister told us that in the last twelve-month period our exports had been greater than in any similar period in the past. That may be true, but those exports are greater, first, because of the huge loans and credits which have been extended by our government; secondly, because of the ERP expenditures made in Canada which I understand will total $800 million this year, and thirdly, because we have not had to face German, Japanese and Czechoslovakian competition in the last few years.
ERP aid will probably be discontinued in the near future and at the same time competition from the countries I have mentioned will become progressively greater. Surely there is no cause for complacency in our trade picture. When he spoke last night even the minister hastened to point out that a decrease in exports was inevitable.
I believe the government has sought alternative markets for our primary products, particularly in the United States, but in spite of that search I think it is safe to assume that our best markets for lumber, wheat, farm products, fruit and the like will continue to be in Great Britain. The one way we can protect that market is to increase British imports. It seems to me that the government has been particularly apathetic in finding methods of increasing those exports.
Last night the minister spent about fifteen minutes telling us about the seriousness of the trade situation. He told us why some action had to be taken to increase British imports. He informed us that the dollar countries would have to remove tariff barriers, and then suddenly when we thought he was

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher going to tell us about the action the government proposed, he changed the subject and was content to say: "This is the situation which we must constantly keep in mind"; the government is "weighing action"; the government is "actively reviewing measures", and so on. In other words, he did not announce any concrete steps. He did not announce any immediate program. He did not make any attempt to translate his words into action of some kind.
Far too often, it seems to me, we in Canada forget that in order to be an exporting country we also have to buy. Our failure to realize that fact has caused a great deal of resentment, and rightly so, in Great Britain. They feel that perhaps Canada is not doing as much as it could to solve the present crisis, which after all is ours, as well as theirs.
Some weeks ago the British took drastic and courageous action to try to get into the North American markets when they devalued the pound. I think it is fair to say that if the tariff barriers on the North American continent had not been so high the British would not have had to devalue to the extent they did. But they brought about that devaluation despite the fact that they knew their cost of living would be forced up. They realized that devaluation was only an initial step which presented no permanent solution. They knew that it would allow them a little time, but if it is to prove of any real value they will have to find a long-term solution.
I suggest that it is in Canada's interest and in the interests of this parliament to help Great Britain find that long-term solution.
The Liberal party so far has failed completely in my opinion to adopt a vigorous import policy. They have been active on exports, but they have not been active in encouraging imports. The government has stood idly by, and is still standing idly by, while the British and European buyer has been gradually choked out of the Canadian market because of a lack of Canadian dollars. Surely it is the duty of parliament to rectify that threat.
I believe it would be in the national interest if this government set up an import board whose duty it would be to encourage British imports and imports from sterling countries, whose duty it would be to take imports now being obtained from the United States and reallocate them to British manufacturers. It is true that a private board was set up this week by a number of private citizens. I believe it is called the dollar-sterling board and is under the chairmanship of Mr. Duncan. We think that is a step in the right direction. It might be of some help, and we hope the government will give it every assistance, including financial aid. But we do not think


it is the final answer. We believe there should be a government board set up with all the support of the government behind it, manned by men who would spend their full time on this problem. This is a step which the C.C.F. party hopes this government will take in order to meet this trade crisis.
If we are as anxious as many have said they are, to give the maximum encouragement to British imports, certainly the time has come to grant the British tariff concessions. It seems to me that government tariff policy in recent years, particularly where Great Britain is concerned, has been very shortsighted. When delivering his budget speech on March 22, 1949, the minister said, as reported on page 1801 of Hansard:
In view of the pending tariff negotiations at Annecy and other trade discussions which are envisaged ... I am not proposing any tariff changes at this time.
He said that in March. That is strange language coming from a minister of a government which for years has paid lip service to the principle of freer trade. Several years ago the Geneva trade agreements were announced in Canada with a great deal of fanfare, but to this moment the government has not presented those agreements to parliament and allowed us to either approve or disapprove of them. As a matter of fact, many of the benefits which would have accrued to Canada from the Geneva agreements were nullified by government embargoes and the like.
The Annecy agreements were tabled several weeks ago but I do not think the most ardent Liberal will suggest that their effect can be anything but minor. About $20 million out of a total of $2 billion will be affected, less than one per cent of our trade. The Annecy trade agreements do not even touch Canada's basic trade problem. The government is only nibbling at the fringe of our trade difficulties. It has been making a great deal of fuss about very little when it talks about the Annecy agreements.
Of course Canadians will welcome the changes, but most of them will realize that the Annecy agreements are only a drop in the proverbial ocean. In his budget speech this March the minister piously said that it was government policy to facilitate the efforts of United Kingdom exporters to regain their historic share of the Canadian market, and that that was particularly so in the case of cotton piece goods. That was a sensible policy, but while in one breath the minister enunciated a policy of helping the British, in the next breath he announced higher tariffs on British textiles. The minister talked one way and acted another. At the very moment when we should be doing something to

increase British imports, at the very moment when lower tariffs are called for, the minister, a minister of a free trade government so-called, brings in higher tariffs. I do not see any consistency in that policy. As a result, British textile manufacturers have found it increasingly difficult to sell to the Dominion of Canada. A Canadian Press dispatch dated October 6 from London bears the following heading:
Tariff on Textiles Termed "Almost Disastrous"
The article quotes a British board of trade official as saying:
Reimposition of a Canadian preferential tariff on British textiles last July has had an "almost disastrous" effect on efforts to sell more cotton and rayon goods in Canada, a board of trade spokesman said yesterday.
Last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said that he was most encouraged and pleased to see President Truman giving leadership where tariffs were concerned. We think it is time that Canada also gave a little bit of leadership. Must we always play follow the leader? At this time we call upon the Liberal party to implement its longstanding pledge of freer trade. We ask for an immediate and substantial downward revision of tariffs on British commonwealth goods and on goods from the sterling areas, first, to allow those nations to earn Canadian dollars to buy our goods, and, second, to help lower the cost of living of the Canadian people.
I know that the Minister of Finance will probably say that such action is not feasible because of the Geneva agreements. I would point out to him in the first place that the Geneva agreements have not been ratified by this parliament. I would point out in the second place that, as I understand the Geneva agreements, there are various escape clauses which can be used to give the British preference if it is necessary, or if there is an emergency. I think there is an emergency today. Lower tariffs then are the second step which the C.C.F. suggests to solve our present trade crisis.
There is one further step which should be taken. During his budget speech the Minister of Finance repeatedly stated that he was opposed to bilateral trade agreements. I must say that I agree with a good deal of what he said. Yet no government can decide on its own what it is going to do and then pursue that policy regardless of the wishes of the nation with which it is trading. It is not a question whether or not we like to trade by bilateral methods. It is a question whether, in order to keep our British markets, we are willing to trade bilaterally if the British wish us to do so. Therefore we think 45781-65J
The Budget-Mr. Low
that, if Great Britain wants to make a bilateral agreement, rather than lose those markets the government should be willing to do so, where it is practical.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier the main criticism which this group has of the budget is its failure to take adequate steps to meet the deteriorating trade situation, and particularly British-Canadian trade. We do not think it is enough for parliament to indulge in talk, drift along, and do nothing, because it lacks a program which will result in action. We urge the government to take the following steps without delay: (1) establish government import boards whose purpose it would be to encourage imports from British and sterling countries generally; (2) reduce substantially tariffs on goods coming from the British commonwealth and sterling area; (3) enter into bilateral agreements with the British if they so desire; (4) endeavour to sign long-term agreements for primary products such as wheat, livestock, fish, lumber, et cetera.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue):
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the word "should" and substituting therefor the following words:
"Give immediate consideration to a reduction of tariffs sufficient to encourage an increase in imports from the United Kingdom and other sterling countries."
Hon. members of the Liberal party will see that there are no strings attached to that amendment. Anyone who believes in freer trade should have no difficulty in voting for it. I call upon my Liberal friends to vote the way they have been talking for the last fifty years.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the financial year is more than half gone, and here we are, the elected representatives of the people of Canada, just now getting down to the consideration of the government's financial policy and program for the fiscal year 1949-50. I think that is an absurd situation. I say that for this reason: In spite of the fact that we as members of the House of Commons, the people's elected representatives, should be exercising control of the purse strings of the nation, the executive have gone ahead for more than seven months with plans of their own for which they have absolutely no legislative sanction whatever.
That is one of the things that lead me' to a conclusion that I want to discuss briefly a little later this afternoon, namely, that Canada is rapidly developing in absolutism. That is a serious situation. It seemed to me that, as the jovial Minister of Finance (Mr,

The Budget-Mr. Low
Abbott) presented his budget speech last night, he emphasized, if not by his actual words at least by a number of implications at several points, that the buoyancy of revenues, the condition of high production, the very satisfactory employment situation, and the general prosperity accompanied by those other circumstances, are entirely the result of the policies that have been pursued by the Liberal party. It seemed to me he suggested that they were all Liberal achievements for which the Liberal government of course quite readily wished to take the credit.
Anyone listening to the minister last night would agree that he was making no unmistakable claim that all these conditions came about as a result of the wise guidance of his colleagues in the cabinet of the Liberal party. Yet it has been my belief all along that the prosperity and the buoyant revenues of the various countries of the world-and by the way Canada has not been the only one which has experienced such things; they have taken place under governments of different stripes, Liberal, Conservative, Socialist, or what not-arose as the result of the action of one Schicklgruber who brought on the war. It is unfortunate that Hitler, who started the war, is the one to whom we nave to give credit for the prosperity we have aad since 1940 and 1941. That is tragic, but t is true nevertheless.
I am quite prepared to give the Liberal government full credit for full employment, revenue buoyancy, debt reduction, high production and prosperity if at the same time they are prepared to take credit for bringing on the war. I wonder if they are prepared to take the responsibility for the suffering and the anguish of the thousands who lost dear ones as a result of the war. I wonder if they are prepared to acknowledge that they are responsible for the tremendous increase in the national debt which has risen from about three and a half billion to around sixteen billion gross since 1938, and the interest burden that rests so heavily on the people, which has risen from approximately $140 million a year to about $450 million. I have not heard them declare that they are ready to take the responsibility for the increase in taxation by more than four times what it was in the last year before the war. I only inject these comments into the introduction of what I have to say by way of a sober reminder that the government must be careful about what it takes credit for, and a sober reminder to the government that most of those things for which they did take credit came about as a result of the circumstances of the times, coupled with the superhuman efforts of all the Canadian people.

In the minister's speech last night, under the heading of "Economic Review", he had this to say:
The latest figure for the wholesale price index is one per cent below a year ago, and for the cost of living index two per cent above a year ago.
Now, sir, during the course of my comments on the budget last spring, I emphasized the tragic results of the minister's failure to do something about the cost of living. It was not impossible for him to deal an effective blow against the continued rise in living costs in this country. At that time I contended, and I still contend, that the government should have overhauled the whole of its tax structure, beginning with the sales tax and other hidden taxes. On a number of occasions in this house, I have shown how the hidden taxation to which the government is addicted gives rise to a deadly upward spiral of consumer prices and the cost of living.
The eight per cent sales tax that is collected by the manufacturers from the wholesalers becomes a part of the wholesaler's cost. His regular mark-up, therefore, has to include the sales tax and so it increases the cost of the goods to the retailer. In due course, the retailer increases his price to the consumer in proportion, so there is a pyramiding effect all the way along through the imposition at different levels of these hidden taxes. It must not be overlooked, Mr. Speaker, that the sales tax is added to the tax paid on imports which further increases the cost of production and prices to the consumer on many items in daily use throughout this country. There are quite a number of other hidden taxes on products which are not called sales taxes. They are added at different levels of production and distribution, but they really have the same effect of pushing up the cost of production. All of these taxes contribute to the almost unbearably high cost of living under which the Canadian people have had to live for a number of years.
Everybody has had to pay these taxes. I contend, sir, that it is unfortunate that they bear more heavily in proportion on the poor than on the rich. These hidden taxes are just another way of freeing the rich from taxation and putting upon the poor the major burden of the taxes that are paid in this country. Even at this late date, the government should have wiped out the sales tax with one stroke. It only brings in, Mr. Speaker, approximately $350 million a year. By eliminating this tax, and by coupling it with action which would have given some concession perhaps to manufacturers and to industry, a very substantial reduction in the cost of living could have been ensured quite quickly.

Instead of this desirable action, last night the minister merely brushed a crumb or two oil the ministerial table for a few of the poor people of this country when he removed the sales tax from fuel oil and cider. Few poor people can buy cider or wine anyway.

In the minister's speech last night, he admitted we do face a trade crisis.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, I made no such statement, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know the minister did not make that statement in so many words. While it is true, Mr. Speaker, that during the recent election campaign the Liberals denied that there was a trade crisis, last night the minister used these words:
Nevertheless, some declines in our overseas export markets have already occurred and some further declines can hardly be avoided. The government will do everything in its power to limit this decline in overseas trade but much will depend on the progress which our overseas customers make in overcoming their dollar difficulties.
This is mild language, sir, that is intended to soften somewhat the seriousness of the whole trade situation that we have been facing, not for just a few weeks but for months. The minister's attendance at both the London and Washington conferences, together with what was done there and the statements he made while he was there, indicate rather more clearly than his words last night the seriousness of this whole situation. By the way, it is not of recent origin; Canada has faced a serious trade crisis for almost a year.
In referring to the two conferences at London and Washington last night, the Minister of Finance referred to the consideration that was given to both long-term and shortterm measures which it was hoped would provide solutions to the trade impasse that has most of the countries of the world thoroughly worried. The minister said the long-term, positive objective must be the achievement of a pattern of world trade in which the dollar and non-dollar countries could live together within one single multilateral system under which a balance would be achieved by the expansion and not the contraction of trade. I believe those are his words.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to our mind that is a most worthy objective. At least, it is a good
The Budget-Mr. Low
start. The minister did not say, however, along what lines the discussion took place in efforts to find ways of achieving that objective. For instance, I should like to ask the minister and perhaps when he does speak in rebuttal he might deign to answer it- although on a number of occasions before we have asked questions which have received only a polite silence from him: Did the representatives at these two conferences, and particularly the Washington conference, consider as one means of getting on the right road towards the adoption of this multilateral type of trade a conversion of goods balances basis rather than the old basis of the convertibility of currencies which has failed? If not, I appeal to the government and the minister to give this idea of multilateral trade on the basis of convertibility of goods balances careful study to see if it would not be possible to adopt it as one means of helping to straighten out this world tangle.
I am sure the minister knows that multilateral trade on a convertibility of currencies basis is at the present time an utter absurdity, and it is likely to remain so until two very important changes have been made in the world. When I say "two important changes'' I refer to the attitude of the United States concerning favourable trade balances, and the fact that international exchanges are and have been in the hands of manipulators who promote currency wars for their own benefit.
Why do I say that multilateral trade based on the convertibility of currencies has failed? In the first place, the convertibility of currencies has been rendered impossible. The whole world has suffered from a shortage of United States dollars which has resulted from the determination of the United States to have a favourable balance of trade year after year. To ensure this, the United States must export more than she is prepared to import each year. Under such circumstances, anyone can see that there can only be one end and that is a world crisis in trade developing out of a shortage of dollars. I should like to illustrate what I mean by quoting some figures which I obtained from the United States embassy showing the amount of American favourable balance of payments for last year. They are as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Largely.

This is exclusive of Marshall aid. These are figures that we obtained from the United States embassy today. If you add the Marshall aid, it brings the total favourable balance for the United States for last year to something around $11 billion. No wonder the world has suffered a shortage of dollars! There could be nothing else under those circumstances.
Surely the whole solution of this problem turns on whether the United States in future will make available to the world an adequate supply of their dollars by balancing her trade with the world. It simply means of course their willingness to import into their country goods which they have purchased with their dollars in the other countries of the world, or to export less; in other words, buying from all of the countries of the world an aggregate of goods and services equal to the aggregate of those same things which they export to the rest of the world. That seems fundamental. But I am convinced that to achieve such a desirable end the commonwealth nations will have to draw closer together and will have to stand side by side, solidly shoulder to shoulder, to provide that balancing factor which is necessary to bring the world successfully out of its terrible position of unbalance in trade. As far as I can see, there can be no other way. It will certainly be necessary to modify or to suspend the most-favoured-nation clause in trade agreements until all the nations have demonstrated their willingness to balance their trade with the rest of the world. That unconditional most-favoured-nation clause will have to be modified.
I should now like to turn to something which is closely allied to this whole situation in trade, and that is the industrial development in our own country. The problem of industrialization cannot be divorced from our trade problems. Canada is twenty-five years behind the times in the development of her resources and her industry. I have here some figures which I obtained recently from our own bureau of statistics; they will indicate what I mean and will drive home the seriousness of this situation.
One of the things which are cluttering up our trade position is this. These figures indicate that last year we purchased from the United States, with cold United States dollars that are so scarce, coal to the value of $203,415,929. We bought in that country and from dollar countries oil to the extent of $187,241,729. We bought steel, raw and manufactured, to the value of $713,126,672, with United States dollars that have been so scarce; and we bought sugar to the extent of $560,551. One of the great reasons why we have been drained, almost bled white, of our reserve of United States dollars is the fact that we have not taken the bold course in developing our own resources and industry to the point where we can supply many of these things ourselves; and there is not anyone here who can deny that we could produce many of these things by ourselves and do so economically.
Canada should be pursuing a most vigorous national policy toward self-sufficiency in the essentials of living so that we can have a goodly measure of independence, a thing we do not possess today. Every time a strike takes place in the United States or in some other country of the world, it makes Canadians go short of things which we could be providing for ourselves. Right today the people of Ontario and Quebec are living in the shadow of fear for this winter because of the coal strike in the United States. Yet all the time we are living in a land that was abundantly blessed by the great Creator who placed right here in our own land forty-nine billion or fifty billion tons of coal that has not been developed.
I know of deposits of coal in large areas in Alberta, where the coal can be mined almost with strip methods at low cost. That is hard coal that can compare quite favourably with coal which we import from Ohio and Pennsylvania. That coal can be brought down and put onto the market of the east, in the central provinces, in competition with coal that is being brought in from the United States. We have lacked the vision or leadership to develop those mines and our transportation facilities so that we could bring that coal down here and satisfy this eastern market, thus making ourselves independent at least to that extent.
What I have said about coal is true of other things, steel in particular. There is no reason in this world why we should be purchasing sugar from any dollar country today or why we should be under that necessity. I say that in times of crisis, in times of stress, Canada must be in a position of independence. We must encourage industrialization to the greatest extent possible and as fast as possible. It must be done on a regional basis
fMr. Low.]

with widespread dispersion for safety's sake in these times. We must see to it also that justice is given to the various regions of Canada where justice has been absent hitherto. My friend the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) dealt to some extent with the problem of devaluation and I do not intend to labour it at all. I spoke about deflation once before and placed our views before the house, but I should like to say just a word about it. I think the minister described it as a short-term measure to improve world trade. It does seem strange, but it is true, that from a world point of view somebody seems to be able to drum up a crisis almost any day. The modern crisis, as revealed by the administrator of our finances last night in his budget speech, is that we are short of dollars. The minister and his counterparts from other countries met in London and in Washington. Evidently they believed that the way to meet the situation was to make dollars dearer, which they proceeded to do by devaluation. This was done evidently on the understanding or in the belief that it would make it possible for Britain to sell more in the United States, and of course to obtain less dollars from the sale. We have to keep that in our minds, and it would also enable Britain and Canada to buy less goods in the United States for more pounds or more Canadian dollars. I suppose one could use up a good many minutes of time discussing the merits or demerits of this whole thing as a short-term objective; but my inclination just now, Mr. Speaker, is not to launch out in discussion of the objectives but to try to probe the question that goes to the very root of our economic discontent of which devaluation is but one of the symptoms.
I speak of the widely held belief that money is and should be treated as a commodity in itself. It is a vicious conception. A mass of evidence to support my contention was placed on record before the banking and commerce committee of this house in 1923, and also before the Macmillan commission in London in 1930, I think it was. Out of the masses of evidence collected in these two hearings one gets clearly that the idea of money as a thing itself to be bought and sold like beans or rice or automobiles was very widely held at that time, and held almost with the fervour of a religion. This accounts for the fact that many of our most respectable Canadian citizens would throw up their hands in holy horror at the suggestion that they use an elastic tape measure; that they can see nothing at all objectionable in a rubber unit of account. That is a thing that is astounding to many of us who have studied this matter. But a rubber unit of account is exactly what
The Budget-Mr. Low
the manipulators have made of the Canadian dollar, of the pound sterling and of the United States dollar. There is a very real objection, sir, to a rubber unit of account. We Social Crediters object to it because it is destroying civilization step by step. Such things as forced devaluation, tariff and other barriers, trade crises, policies of unemployment and depression, poverty in the midst of plenty, and wars, all have their roots in the frantic effort to keep people thinking and acting as if the unit of our money is a commodity, and a rubber one at that, which can be stretched or contracted in almost unlimited degree to suit the whims of the propagandists who are the only beneficiaries of the system.
We Social Crediters strenuously object to that concept of money. We contend that money, the chief mechanism for distributing goods and services, should be looked upon and treated as units of account. We believe further that until such a financial policy, that is a financial policy based on that concept, is built and applied faithfully in this country, as well as in other countries of the world, there can be little hope for solving the problems of world trade or of the economic ills that confront us today.
History reveals that the root of the success of parliamentary institutions in the past has been that parliament controlled the purse strings of the nation. Resistance to the divine right of kings in the day of that policy, or to any totalitarian policy of any day, has been successful only where the people have kept control of their own money, and where the executive never got control of the purse or of any attributes of that purse or nation. A mass of evidence is available to support the view that since 1914 governments, including the Canadian government, have been moving toward absolutism.
As I mentioned earlier in my remarks, the people of this country no longer control the purse strings, nor their own money. The executive have usurped that control. Some effective way will have to be found, and applied very soon, of stemming this trend or the Canadian people will one day wake up as vassals of a supreme state. Perhaps the most effective remedy would be the institution, in this house particularly, of a responsible vote, independent responsible vote, that would pin any loss resulting from the exercise of it on the voting members, and not on the nation or on political opponents of the government in power. If this can be achieved then, sir, the way can be cleared for a reasonably incorruptible money of account, which is simply a policy that would ensure that all currency and credit in circulation in our land would be fully covered by wealth and readily exchanged for it under a

The Budget-Mr. Low
reasonably stabilized pricing technique. We have that technique and we propose it and are prepared to advance it wherever it is possible and necessary.
Let me emphasize this point, sir. A practical solution of the crises with which we are now faced all over the world can be reached through the development in each and all countries of a science of consumption that is not based on taxation. A solution cannot be reached by restricting consumption, nor by living a life of austerity, nor by maintaining a heavy weight of taxation.
In conclusion, sir, just a word about this whole situation of business recession. Only a short statement was made in the budget speech relative to the government's program for meeting the business recessions or depressions which may face us in the years ahead. I noted that housing construction and the construction of the trans-Canada highway were mentioned, but only in a general and nebulous way. The minister admitted the possibility of economic trouble in Canada as a result of possible failure of foreign markets for Canada's production. Surpluses of many of our products are already visible. The past summer I visited one section, Yarrow, British Columbia, where I saw all of the 1947 crop of berries stored in 400-pound barrels in the basement of a jam factory. Think of it! All of the 1947 crop of berries; and all of the 1948 crop of berries were stored outside the railway right of way in 400-pound barrels. They were lying out there in the blazing sun to rot. It was estimated at that time that fully the equivalent of a million cases of pure strawberry and raspberry jam was lying there and could not be sold at any price.
In storage in Canada we have 48,000,000 pounds of butter, much of which is surplus to our need. The condensed and powdered milk situation, as has already been mentioned, is becoming serious. These and many other item that could be cited indicate the way the wind is blowing. Let it not be forgotten that any unsaleable surpluses on the shelves in the storehouses of the nation usually precede unemployment and depression, with poverty in the midst of plenty. We think that so far the government has been so busy playing politics that it has neglected to draft and bring forward any adequate program of action to cushion the Canadian economy against possible depressions. In the United States President Truman has taken leadership in this matter, and through a committee he has set up has assured the nation that the United States has something ready, in case of difficulty. I hold in my hand "U.S. News and World Report" of October 14, 1949, and at page 18 I find a reference to the Truman ten-year plan,

described by the magazine as The Fair Deal Goal. Evidently it was issued under the direction of Leon Keyserling, vice-chairman of the council of economic advisers, and the No. 1 White House adviser on economic issues who, according to the magazine, has spelled out the fair deal goals for use by the President and the party in power.
The article goes on to say:
If the goals are realized, everybody is going to be well fed, well housed, well clothed.
That is a worthy objective, and evidently it has been developed to a certain degree, and in some detail, through a proposed program of action to ensure that this goal is reached. For example I notice that their 1949 level of production in the United States is approximately $260 billion. Under the fair deal goal they propose to stimulate production so as to bring it up to the $350 billion level. Ninety billion dollars of increased production they propose to use in the following ways: $45 billion is to go toward raising the living standard of two-thirds of American families to a $4,000 minimum. This is physically possible, and if it is physically possible we contend it must be and can be made financially possible.
Then I notice that $12 billion of the excess $90 billion is to go toward health insurance, old age pensions, unemployment benefits and aid to the needy, to ensure that they may have a future without fear.
I see that $2 billion is to be used for the development of natural resources. In connection with this I notice that the Reconstruction Finance Corporation made a huge loan of $34,400,000 to the Kaiser-Frazer Company to make plans for a new low-priced automobile in that country. That is a substantial amount, and will go far toward stimulating the development required if production is to be increased to the extent of $90 billion.
Then, $2 billion is to go to the nation's school system by way of federal aid to education-the very subject we were discussing the other night as being vitally necessary to our country, if we are going to remove some of the inequalities suffered by children in various parts of the country.
Then, $6 billion is to go toward housing, part for slum clearance and part for city planning.
The last item of $23 billion is for the improvement of public roads and for plant improvement.
These figures indicate that they are not asleep down there; they have a plan. They have at least an objective that has been worked out in detail. I am a great believer in objectives, and in my view we should

plead with our government in the months between now and the next session of parliament to develop their program in detail. They should make a statement of the objectives by which they hope to stave off any ill effects of the economic difficulties of other lands, and to cushion the Canadian economy against the impact of such disturbances abroad.
In concluding I would say that the people of Canada would like to be able to face the years ahead with a feeling that their government has taken every possible precaution to protect their economy against the impacts of disturbances elsewhere, wherever they may be. They have every right to expect their government to bring forward the details of their program for ensuring to every Canadian the opportunity to obtain for himself and his family a reasonably high standard of living- just as high as our abundant resources can make possible.
I appeal to the government to prepare carefully and to bring before the next session of parliament a comprehensive program of sound and adequate proposals for reform, for social justice and for national development and security, so that our people can feel like driving ahead, in confidence that everything possible has been done to remove fear and worry, and the spectre of needless suffering.
On motion of Mr. Weir the debate was adjourned.

speechtext:
The answer to the hon. member's question is no.
The purposes of the bill are twofold, first to acquire the external telecommunication assets of Canadian Marconi Company Limited
Overseas Telecommunication Act and Cable and Wireless Limited in Canada and, secondly, to establish a crown company in order to co-ordinate the maintenance and operation of these two commonwealth-controlled telecommunication systems.
Before going into the details of the bill, may I be permitted to say that the assets it is intended to expropriate under the bill are, with respect to the Canadian Marconi Company Limited, the following:
Their receiving station at Yamachiche; their transmitting station at Drummondville; the building and equipment at Montreal; and certain small holdings at Toronto and Vancouver.
Dealing next with Cable and Wireless Limited, the following:
Land, buildings and equipment at Barn-field; electrical equipment at Halifax, Montreal and Harbour Grace; certain furniture and stationery at Toronto and Vancouver.

subtopic: CORPORATION TO TAKE OVER PROPERTY AND EQUIPMENT OF MARCONI AND CABLE AND WIRELESS LIMITED
speechtext: Nothing in Newfoundland?

subtopic: CORPORATION TO TAKE OVER PROPERTY AND EQUIPMENT OF MARCONI AND CABLE AND WIRELESS LIMITED
speechtext:
Yes, at Harbour Grace. The total value of these assets should not exceed $4 million, as set out in the bill-the additional $500,000 referred to in the bill being required for working capital. No assets are to be acquired which relate to the manufacturing, radio broadcasting and ship-to-shore activities of Canadian Marconi Company Limited. And I should like to dispel immediately any impression that what is being taken over is a liability. As I have stated already, the telecommunications side of Canadian Marconi showed a substantial profit in 1948.
These assets are being taken over for two reasons: First, because it is important that we should have control over these services for strategic purposes, and, second, because for many years the telecommunication services controlled by Cable and Wireless and their policies were not acceptable to the commonwealth countries. For the reasons already stated, which it is unnecessary to repeat at this time, and because of meetings which finally culminated in the commonwealth telecommunications convention in London, it was decided to proceed on this basis, namely, that each commonwealth country would take over the telecommunication assets in its own territory.

subtopic: CORPORATION TO TAKE OVER PROPERTY AND EQUIPMENT OF MARCONI AND CABLE AND WIRELESS LIMITED
speechtext: What is to be done with the cables as distinct from the cable stations?

subtopic: CORPORATION TO TAKE OVER PROPERTY AND EQUIPMENT OF MARCONI AND CABLE AND WIRELESS LIMITED
speechtext:
This bill does not provide for the expropriation of cables, only for the expropriation of the assets I mentioned earlier in my statement. Why is it done in that way? I suppose it could be done by setting up a
1034	HOUSE OF
Overseas Telecommunication Act division in one of the departments of government, but after giving that careful consideration it was thought that as these operations would compete with other operations it would be better to set up a crown company. Furthermore, we would like to continue these telecommunication facilities as they were operated heretofore. We feel that the best way to accomplish that is by means of a crown corporation.
Some mention was made that this is likely to create a monopoly. I have looked at the figures mentioned by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in so far as the control of Cable and Wireless is concerned. I believe the leader of the opposition was correct in stating that the move to nationalize commonwealth telecommunication facilities would result in control to the extent of some eighty per cent of the cable system by the British government. I should like to remind the house that the other twenty per cent is quite active. There is keen competition from the United States companies I mentioned before, the Anglo-American Cable Company and the Commercial Cable Company, both of which conduct telecommunication services to and from Canada. Because of that I do not believe that this bill will create a monopoly in any sense.
The bill may be divided into five parts. First, it establishes the crown company; second, it states the powers and purposes of the company; third, it provides it with staff; fourth, it defines its financial requirements and limitations; and, lastly, it stipulates the rules and regulations to govern its operation.
A portion of the bill provides for the appointment of five directors. One director will be the president and general manager and the governor in council will have the power to fix his salary as well as that of the vice-president. I should say at this point that these men will be appointed for a period of seven years. Of the other four directors, one is to be appointed for one year, one for two years and two for three years. These men will receive fees for attending directors' meetings only, and no salary.
It is stated in the bill that the corporation is to be an agent of the crown with restrictions on entering into certain agreements. For instance, the corporation may not without the approval of the governor in council enter into an agreement involving an expenditure of more than $50,000. It may not, without the approval of the governor in council, enter into for a period exceeding three years any agreement or lease that involves an expenditure in any year of more than $5,000. Finally, it may not without such approval acquire any real or personal property, the cost of acquisition of which exceeds the sum of $50,000, or


in any manner dispose of any such property having an original or book value exceeding the sum of $5,000.
Under another portion of the bill the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is authorized to advance the corporation the amount of money mentioned earlier in my statement, $4,500,000, for the purpose of taking over these assets and to provide working capital. The Minister of Finance may also lend the corporation money for temporary purposes not exceeding $100,000. The crown corporation must pay interest on capital advances and deliver certificates of indebtedness for the amounts of money that are lent from time to time by the Minister of Finance. If funds in excess of the requirements exist they are to be paid into the treasury and if there is a deficit on the operations it will be voted in accordance with the usual practice by means of an item in the estimates. The bill provides for an audit and the usual annual report.
During the discussion on the resolution several hon. members, particularly the leader of the opposition, suggested that it would be well to send this bill to a committee. I have no feeling one way or another. If the house feels it would be preferable to send the bill to a committee, I am quite willing to concur in that suggestion. After the debate on the second reading has been concluded and if the motion is approved I would move that the bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, if that is the wish of the house.

subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, October 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fulton for the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Criminal Code (portrayal of crimes).

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I preface my statement tonight with congratulations to the mover of this amendment and to all those who have taken part in a high-class debate, including the hon. members for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) and Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who have supported this amendment with misgivings of the most honourable and intelligent kind. The action of those members, and of the house itself so far, has been an example of sensitivity to public opinion and concern for the

common weal which our democratic system displays when it is functioning properly.
This is not the first time this matter has come up. The hon. member who introduced it referred in the debate to the action which he took in connection with this matter during the time of my distinguished predecessor, the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley. I suppose it can be said that we have not been hasty in acting in this matter, either as a government or as a parliament. There may be those indeed who would say we were dilatory. But I am sure, sir, that all the members of this house, regardless of party, would deliberate most anxiously before taking any action against freedom of expression by writers or artists. But when publishers and disseminators of various kinds of crime comics and obscene literature are heartened and emboldened by this concern of ours for the preservation of literary and artistic freedom, and become steadily more impudent in their degradation of that freedom so that they transform freedom into licence, the time comes, and I think we all agree that it has come, when we must take further action to curtail their offences.
I therefore rise tonight, not only to support the amendment which has been offered by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) but also to suggest that, to be effective, we must go further than this amendment does. With great deference, I do not think that the mere passage of this amendment will, of itself, cure the situation. I should like to offer some suggestions as to how, in my opinion, the code may be strengthened so that this amendment and section 207, of which after it is passed, it will become a part, will become more enforceable. The suggestion which I will make will have certain inherent and unavoidable defects to which some members will no doubt object on grounds which I will admit in advance are very good grounds. In my view, we are faced in this matter with a rather unpleasant dilemma. Either we shal. follow the course which I shall suggest, with all its faults, or we may avoid those faults by letting matters stand in the present unsatisfactory condition.
The amendment we are discussing now, sir, deals only with crime comics, but I think it may be said that the debate has made it quite clear, as it has developed, that at least equally offensive and at least equally injurious to the morals of our youth is the rising tide of pornography which has flooded the bookstands of this country for some time past. The few samples of this which have come to my attention, thanks to the courtesy of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) and which he tells me are fair samples, have

Criminal Code
no redeeming features of any kind; no distinction of conception or style; no humour; no sentiment; certainly no idealism; not even any genuine realism; nothing but hack-work filth seeking filthy lucre.
While no judge of such matters I should have thought, sir, that the influence of these obscene books and magazines would probably be worse than the crime comics. Yet these obscene books and magazines are now covered by section 207 of the Criminal Code and have been covered by that section for over half a century. This provision was first enacted, in, it is true, a slightly different form, in 1892. It was elaborated upon somewhat in 1900; re-enacted in the revised statutes of 1906, and enacted in its present form in 1909. During the whole of this interval prior to 1909, and since 1909 continuously until now, obscene literature has been covered by this section. Yet, sir, judging by the mass of evidence which the members of this house have brought forward in this debate alone, section 207 does not now seem to have been any great deterrent to the production or sale of this obscene literature.
Obscene books and magazines are covered by section 207. Crime comics are not covered -indeed, the purpose of this amendment is to have them covered by that section. Yet the obscene books seem to flourish at least as much as the crime comics. It is significant, I think, that in reply to an inquiry recently made by our department, Nova Scotia could not recall any prosecutions within the last ten years; Prince Edward Island, no prosecutions since 1942; New Brunswick, no information available of any such prosecution within the last five years; Ontario, a few prosecutions which usually failed because of the word "knowingly" or because the jury ruled against the obscenity element. Manitoba had no general statistics, but there were eight prosecutions in Winnipeg since the beginning of 1946 and none at all from 1944 to 1946 inclusive. In Alberta, there were about ten prosecutions in the last five years, while British Columbia recalled only one conviction within five years in respect of moving pictures. Prosecution considered in other cases was dropped because of this word "knowingly" and also a feeling that the persons who should be prosecuted were the publishers in eastern Canada. Of all the provinces of which we made inquiry and which I have named, Quebec, with one hundred prosecutions in the last five years, is the only one in which there has been prosecution on that scale which would seem to be warranted by the observations which have been made in this debate by the members who took part in it.
Now, sir, this amendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops, when passed, will merely bring crime comics as paragraph (d) under the same section 207 of the code of which paragraph (a) now makes the publication and sale of obscene literature an offence. This is all that Bill No. 10 does; and if the experience in regard to obscene literature is any criterion, it is certainly not enough.
I admit I am not a criminal lawyer nor an expert in these matters, but it must be obvious even to lay members of this assembly that the great likelihood is that the crux of this matter is in certain words in the beginning of section 207, which reads as follows:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who-
And these are the words.
-knowingly, without lawful justification or excuse . . .
publishes or sells obscene literature or, as we now seek to have it amended, crime comics and so on. In my judgment it is these words, "knowingly, without lawful justification or excuse," which would appear to make conviction so difficult and prosecution so apparently hopeless that but few prosecutions have been started.
Yet the reason for including these words in the description of the offence is, I submit, a good one.
On the face of it, it seems most unfair, in any country that has the conception of civil liberty that we in Canada have, that a bookseller, who in the ordinary course of his business sells thousands of books that he can never hope to read or to censor himself, should be convicted of an indictable offence and be liable to two years' imprisonment- for what, sir? For selling merchandise like chairs or boxes of soda biscuits that are all alike? No, for selling a book which is unlike the thousands of other books which he sells and which, without any necessary knowledge or fault on his part may, for all he knows, be obscene. It is therefore unjust and unfair to the honest bookseller that these words "knowingly, without lawful justification or excuse" should be absent from the definition of the offence. Yet when to protect the honest bookseller-and the law should protect honest people-these words are inserted in the definition of the offence, it apparently becomes-next to impossible to convict a dishonest bookseller; for, if he is prosecuted, all he has to do is to maintain a naive and wideeyed innocence of any knowledge of the contents of the books that he has sold in the ordinary course of business, in order to establish a good defence to the prosecution.

Criminal Code
It may then be asked: Why not prosecute the publisher? Surely he must read what he publishes.
There are two points to be noted with regard to this suggestion, the first of which is this. I am credibly informed that a good [DOT]deal of the publishing of this kind of literature in Canada consists in printing it in Canada from plates made in the United States; and it is conceivable-although in my opinion not at all likely-that the Canadian publisher may run off this print job of a particular book-for example, the one upon which the prosecution against him may be based- as a routine business without informing himself of its text. Under those circumstances he could come into court, and if he could persuade the magistrate that he did not know it was an offence, then he would escape conviction.

subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
speechtext: That he did not know it was an offence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
speechtext:
I beg hon. members pardon. If he could persuade the magistrate that he did not know that the book he was publishing was obscene he would escape conviction.
In the case of crime comics the publisher would have difficulty in escaping knowledge. Thus, while the publisher could plead a lack of knowledge in the same way as the bookseller, this defence upon the part of the publisher, I think we must all agree, would seem to be much more difficult to maintain and to establish than upon the part of the bookseller.
The second point in connection with this suggestion-why not prosecute the publisher? -is, I think, a somewhat more difficult one. While this parliament, as a federal parliament enacts the criminal law, the enforcement of that law is exclusively a provincial right and provincial duty. Therefore, if he is prosecuted, the publisher can move his operations-and if they simply consist of printing from plates that are brought in from the United States it would not be a matter of great difficulty to move them-into and seek sanctuary in a province where the police and the law enforcement officers are less diligent in the enforcement of section 207.
At this point, in justice to the government of which I am a member, to my distinguished predecessors in this high office, to the officers of the Department of Justice and, I think, to truth itself, I feel that I must indulge in some plain speaking. The constitutional responsibilities of the federal parliament, and the federal government on the one hand and of the provincial legislatures or the provincial governments on the other, are in this matter as plain as a pikestaff. To the federal government is assigned, as class 27 of section 91

of the British North America Act, the power to make laws with regard to:
The criminal law, except the constitution of courts of criminal jurisdiction, but including the procedure in criminal matters.
To the provincial governments and the provincial legislatures is assigned as class 14 of section 92 of the British North America Act:
The administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance, and organization of provincial courts, both of civil and of criminal jurisdiction, and including procedure in civil matters in those courts.
I know that we lawyers are twitted, even in this parliament, for raising this matter of constitutional law when other matters such as the one we are discussing are brought up for discussion. I know that the courts have difficulty in determining whether certain subject matters fall under federal or provincial jurisdiction. But so far as I know there has never been any doubt or controversy over the division between federal and provincial jurisdiction in this field of criminal law. The enforcement of criminal law, as distinguished from its enactment, is neither a federal responsibility nor a federal right. There is no federal invasion of provincial rights which would be more quickly and more justly resented than that which would take place if the federal Minister of Justice were to go into a province over the head of its attorney general who, under our constitution, is its chief law enforcement officer, in order to enforce law and administer justice there, not in the name of the provincial attorney general but in the name of the federal Minister of Justice. I cannot recall a single case in Canadian history where the federal minister of justice has ever done such a thing. Quite obviously it would be the gravest sort of reflection upon both the integrity and the competence of the provincial attorney general were the Minister of Justice to do so.
Now, sir, there has been what, from my point of view, I must regard as a rather regrettable tendency on one or two occasions in this debate to imply at least shall I say, and in some cases to state explicitly, that it is the federal Department of Justice which is responsible for and has been remiss in the enforcement of section 207. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) made an excellent presentation of his viewpoint in this debate, and to him I am particularly indebted for the loan of his file of samples, without which our staff would have had much greater difficulty in dealing with this matter. It pains me to have to make the remarks that I am about to make, but in fairness to ourselves I think they must be made. I am sure that it was unintentional that the hon. member, during the course of a speech which

was in every other respect an admirable one, made this remark. He said, as reported at page 518 of Hansard:
Might I emphasize once again that, apart from crime comics if the Minister of Justice, who has the administration of the R.C.M.P. under his department, or if the various cities with their own police forces would take that section of the criminal code and enforce it, sending a few of these publishers to jail for a couple of years. I have no doubt but what it would make a difference in the type of publications in this country.
I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that with a part of that statement I am in agreement. Very probably the result which my hon. friend envisages here would come about. I have not the slightest doubt that sending a few of these gentlemen to jail would have an effect upon that type of publication in the country. But the point I wish to emphasize is that this action is not within our federal power and it is not our federal responsibility.
Even the reference to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is misleading. It is quite true that they are administered under the Department of Justice, but in that capacity the only offences that they prosecute under my authority as Minister of Justice are offences like those under the Foreign Exchange Control Act, the Excise Act and similar federal statutes.
The governments of Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and several other provinces, under an arrangement that is in the highest degree in the interest of the taxpayers of this country, pay to this government a large sum of money for the use of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in these various provinces. Having only one police force to administer both federal and provincial law is much more economical; but what is more important is that it commands a much greater respect for law enforcement and for the administration of justice. But, sir, if under the guise of this police contract, we were, by the control which we exercise through the Justice department over the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to try to siphon away provincial rights by attempting to direct the mounted police in respect of those matters upon which they are supposed to take directions from the attorneys general of the provinces, it would not be long before the provinces would refuse to renew these police contracts. The plain fact of the matter is that the agreement which covers the renting of these police services to the provinces specifies that, when the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are engaged in the enforcement of all of these laws which come under provincial enforcement, they are the instrument not of the Minister of Justice but of the provincial attorney general and subject wholly to the
Criminal Code
latter's control. For that reason, the exhortations and the strictures of the hon. member for Macleod should be addressed not to me but to his good friend, the attorney general of Alberta. When I say that I want to make myself perfectly clear that I am implying no criticism of the attorney general of Alberta, who is an equally good friend of mine.
It may very well be that in that province, under conditions with which I am not familiar, the words "knowingly, without lawful justification or excuse" in section 207 would make it hard to secure a conviction against the booksellers in Alberta. One of the things that the prosecution has to take into account in this connection is that in offences of this nature against morals nothing is worse from every standpoint than an abortive prosecution. To the offender and to the offending publication the advertising value of an unsuccessful prosecution is simply beyond price. I believe it is said that Mae West claimed she got her start in life from having been so prosecuted. Therefore, sir, if there are no such publishers in Alberta- and my information is that there are none- it is not difficult to understand that the crown prosecutors in that province, like the crown prosecutors in those other provinces whose statistics I mentioned a few moments ago, will not be over-enthusiastic about taking on the difficult task of prosecuting Alberta retailers of books, when the crown prosecutors of other provinces have not done anything in the apparently easier task of prosecuting publishers within their jurisdiction.
The debate upon this amendment has shown that upon the one hand there is a huge volume of pornographic literature exposed for sale upon the newsstands of this country and, upon the other, that in relation to this huge volume of exposure and sale there have been in all of the provinces except one a relatively small number of prosecutions. It seems to me, as I have indicated before, that the apparent reason for this inconsistency is most likely to be found in these words "knowingly, without lawful justification or excuse."

subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
speechtext: Will the minister allow one question? What would be a lawful justification or excuse?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend will wait just a moment I shall come to that.

subtopic: PORTRAYAL OF CRIMES BY PICTURES IN MAGAZINES, ETC., TENDING TO INDUCE VIOLENCE
